h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר י״א Parshas Zachor — Maamar Yud Aleph

p: "Outside they wander and do not enter,
these brazen dogs" (the hymn Bnei Heichala).
בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב בְּשַׁלַּח סד, ב)
"Fortunate are you who sow beside all waters,
who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey" —
these are two crowns of the left side
דַּאֲחִידָן בְּהוּ עַמִּין עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת
to which the idolatrous nations hold fast,
which are called ox and donkey;
and this is what is written (Bereishis 32:6):
and they cannot rule over them;
this is what is written, "who send forth...."
the two kelipos of Esav and Yishmael,
from which the seventy kelipos branched out,
The kelipah of Yishmael is lusts
for so it is written of the Egyptians,
"whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys," etc.
for they were steeped in lewdness.
"with a people that resembles a donkey";
and these were Eliezer and Yishmael
And slaves are steeped in lewdness,
and Yishmael was the son of a maidservant from Egypt,
and therefore he is likened to a donkey.
and it is stated (Midrash Rabbah, Balak 20:14)
that this is the most foolish of animals...;
וְכֵן הַלָּשׁוֹן בַּגְּמָרָא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא עד, א)
And so is the expression in the Gemara (Bava Basra 74a):
that it is not common for there to emerge
that is, they are haughty toward the public in their wisdom,
And the donkey is the most foolish of animals, as mentioned above.
And lust is an act of folly,
"Shittim — for they engaged in matters of folly";
"A person does not commit a transgression
אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנַס בּוֹ רוּחַ שְׁטוּת
unless a spirit of folly has entered him,
For there is no folly greater than this,
for it is a loathsome thing,
"A woman is a skin-bag full of filth...";
and this fool loses his world
for one moment of repulsive lust.
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא קְלִיפַּת יִשְׁמָעֵאל דְּתַאֲוָה
Therefore the kelipah of Yishmael, the kelipah of lust, is called
And the kelipah of Esav — envy and murder —
עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת סא, א)
that an animal has an evil inclination,
for we see that it does damage,
And corresponding to them Yaakov said,
וַיְהִי לִי שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר [בְּרֵאשִׁית לב, ו]
And it is stated in the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 5b):
their inclination is given over into their hands,
'Fortunate are you who sow beside all waters';
and 'sowing' means nothing other than charity, etc.,
and 'water' means nothing other than Torah, etc."
"who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey":
"Whoever engages in Torah and acts of kindness
merits the inheritance of two tribes, etc.:
his enemies fall before him, like Yosef, etc.,
and he merits understanding, like Yissachar";
כִּי יוֹסֵף הַיְינוּ גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים וּצְדָקָה
For Yosef is kindness and charity
the opposite of the kelipah of Esav,
עַל פָּסוּק דָּם שָׂנֵאתָ [יְחֶזְקֵאל לה, ו]
"You hated the blood of a man in his body";
and he is evil to people.
Regarding Esav and Amalek it is written (Devarim 25:18),
while regarding Yosef it is written (Bereishis 42:18),
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכג, ב)
that the offspring of Esav is delivered
only into the hand of the offspring of Yosef.
Esav is a murderer and a robber,
while regarding Yosef it is written (Bereishis 47:12),
and on account of this he is called Kalkol
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִדְרָשׁ חֻקַּת רַבָּה ט, א; תַּנְחוּמָא ו)
(as stated in Midrash Chukas Rabbah 9:1; Tanchuma 6),
for he fed and sustained people.
He, in holiness, stands against the kelipah of Esav,
as they said in the Gemara.
And Yissachar, in holiness, stands against the kelipah of Yishmael,
שֶׁיִּשְׁמָעֵאל עוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשֵׂה שְׁטוּת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
for Yishmael commits acts of folly, as mentioned above.
וּבְיִשָּׂשכָר כְּתִיב [דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א יב, לג]
Regarding Yissachar it is written (I Divrei HaYamim 12:33),
"You will not find a young scholar who issues rulings
unless he comes, etc., from the tribe of Yissachar."
And this is engagement in Torah,
for this is the portion of Yissachar,
just as a donkey carries the burden,
This is the opposite of the donkey of the kelipah.
For he is like a donkey for the load,
and the burden nullifies the desire of lust;
drag him to the beis midrash" —
that is, the evil inclination of lust,
which is called "repulsive," as mentioned above;
so that it becomes desire and longing for Torah,
as it will remain in the future
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קלח, א בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם)
(as stated in Zohar vol. 1, 138a, in the Midrash HaNe'lam).
And those who engage in Torah and acts of kindness —
their inclination is given over into their hands,
And this is what they said (Avodah Zarah, ibid.),
בָּתַר הָךְ דִּמְשַׁלְּחֵי רֶגֶל הַשּׁוֹר וְהַחֲמוֹר
right after that teaching of "who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey":
upon words of Torah like an ox to the yoke
and like a donkey to the load" —
הַיְינוּ לְהַכְנִיס שְׁנֵי הַכֹּחוֹת אֵלּוּ לִקְדוּשָּׁה
that is, to bring these two forces into holiness.
and "like an ox to the yoke,"
for the yoke is placed on the ox
so that it cannot gore with its head.
"Behold, I deliver you to the dog" —
[הַגָּהוֹת עַל הַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ שָׁם אוֹת א]
(Haggahos on the holy Zohar, ibid., os 1)
that the inner letters of shor and chamor —
the vav of shor and the mem-vav of chamor —
equal in gematria the word kelev, dog.
And this is the kelipah of Amalek,
it stands against the holiness of Atika:
just as that is above the grasp of human intellect,
so the kelipah of Amalek is against reason,
כְּמוֹ שָׁם אַחַר קְרִיעַת יַם סוּף
as there, after the splitting of the Sea,
דִּכְתִיב [שְׁמוֹת טו, יד] שָׁמְעוּ עַמִּים יִרְגָּזוּן
where it is written (Shemos 15:14), "Nations heard and trembled,"
and "no spirit remained any longer in any man,"
yet he paid no heed to this.
Now on Shabbos there is a revelation of Atika.
On the day of Shabbos the revelation is still concealed,
when the Forehead of Atika is revealed
when the aspect of Atika comes into revelation —
that is, the light of the Countenance —
then the kelipah of Amalek is nullified,
for it becomes clear that Yisrael
are bound to the root of holiness.
And then "Outside they wander and do not enter,
the kelipah of Amalek is nullified,
for Yisrael merit to be bound to the root
and to "the light of the King's Countenance, which is life."

paragraphs.text: Bnei Heichala, zemer for the third Shabbos meal — “Rejoice now, at this hour, in which there is favor and no anger. Outside they go and do not enter, those brazen dogs. He will place them in their holes, and they will hide among the rocks.” The stanza describes the removal of accusing forces during the hour of divine favor. Rav Tzadok’s identification of those forces with Amalek explains the zemer through the Zohar passage that follows.

paragraphs.text: Yevamot 62a — “Rav said: All agree that a slave has no recognized paternal lineage, for it is written, ‘Stay here with the donkey’—a people likened to the donkey.” The Gemara is addressing the legal recognition of lineage in slavery through the wordplay im/am. Rav Tzadok applies the traditional animal image to an inner trait; the source’s immediate legal context should remain clear.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 26:7 — “Rabbi Aivu said: Two people practiced proper conduct, Avraham and Shaul. Of Avraham it says, ‘Avraham rose early in the morning and took his two young men with him.’ Who were they? Yishmael and Eliezer. Of Shaul it says, ‘He went, and two men with him.’ Who were they? Avner and Amasa.” The Midrash’s topic is taking companions on a journey. It identifies the two men left with the donkey in the Akedah account.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 113b — “Canaan commanded his sons five things: Love one another; love robbery; love sexual immorality; hate your masters; and do not speak truth.” This list is the cited rabbinic portrait of Canaan’s instruction, from which Rav Tzadok takes the particular connection with unrestrained desire.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah, Balak 20:14 — “This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, cares for the honor of creatures and knows their needs, and therefore closed the animal’s mouth. Had it spoken, people could neither subdue it nor stand against it: this was the most foolish of animals and he the wisest of the wise, yet once it spoke he could not stand against it.” The Midrash contrasts Bilam’s pretended mastery with the humiliation of being answered by his donkey. Rav Tzadok selects the animal’s description as an image of foolishness.

paragraphs.text: Rashbam on Bava Basra 74a, s.v. Kol Abba and Chamra — “‘Every Abba is a donkey’: Rabbah bar bar Chanah is Rabbi Abba bar Chanah, just as Ravina is Rav Avina. ‘A donkey’—that is, a fool like a donkey.” In the narrative a traveling companion rebukes Rabbah bar bar Chanah after he fails to count the tzitzis before returning a garment. Rashbam explains the pun on his name.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 81a — “Why is it not common for Torah scholars’ sons to become Torah scholars? Rav Yosef said: So that they should not say Torah is an inheritance for them. Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi said: So that they should not elevate themselves above the community. Mar Zutra said: Because they lord themselves over the community. Rav Ashi said: Because they call people ‘donkeys.’” The passage criticizes arrogance toward the public. It is not an endorsement of using the animal term to degrade other people.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 106a — “What is the meaning of ‘Shittim’? Rabbi Eliezer says: Shittim was its name. Rabbi Yehoshua says: They engaged in acts of foolishness.” This is the wordplay on the setting of Israel’s transgression with Moav. It stands beside the Gemara’s interpretation of Rephidim as slackening in Torah, already cited in the preceding maamar.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 3a — “Reish Lakish said: A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of foolishness has entered him, as it says, ‘If a man’s wife turns astray’—tisteh is written.” The derashah relates turning astray to foolishness. Rav Tzadok explains desire as a distortion in judgment that sacrifices enduring good for a passing moment.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 152a — “Rav Kahana said: What is meant by ‘For He spoke and it was’? This is a wife. ‘He commanded and it stood’—these are children. It was taught: A woman is a skin-bag filled with excrement, and her opening filled with blood, yet all pursue her.” The teaching occurs in a discussion of aging and the divinely implanted force of sexual attraction. Rav Tzadok invokes its bodily image against the illusion that desire’s momentary object is worth losing one’s spiritual world.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 75:12 — “‘I have an ox and a donkey.’ The ox is Yosef, as it says, ‘His firstborn ox has majesty.’ The donkey is Yissachar, as it says, ‘Yissachar is a strong-boned donkey.’ Yosef’s descendant will arise to destroy Amalek, as it says, ‘Yehoshua weakened Amalek and his people by the sword.’ Yissachar’s sons know what the Holy One, blessed be He, does in His world, as it says, ‘Of the sons of Yissachar, those who understand the times, to know what Israel should do.’” The Midrash already pairs Yosef’s victory over Amalek with Yissachar’s understanding. Rav Tzadok shows how both images can be redirected into holiness.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 5b — “Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Benaah’s name: What does ‘Fortunate are you who sow beside all waters, sending away the foot of the ox and donkey’ mean? Fortunate are Israel: When they engage in Torah and acts of kindness, their inclination is delivered into their hands, rather than they being delivered into its hands. Sowing means charity, as it says, ‘Sow righteousness for yourselves and reap according to kindness.’ Water means Torah, as it says, ‘All who are thirsty, go to water.’” Torah and kindness are the paired practices through which the forces represented by ox and donkey become subject to the person.

paragraphs.text: Bava Kamma 17a — “One merits the inheritance of two tribes: The enclosure of Yosef, as it says, ‘Yosef is a fruitful son; daughters tread upon the wall,’ and Yissachar’s inheritance, as it says, ‘Yissachar is a strong-boned donkey.’ Some say: His enemies fall before him as before Yosef, as it says, ‘With them he shall gore peoples together to the ends of the earth’; and he merits understanding like Yissachar, as it says, ‘Of the sons of Yissachar, those who understand the times, to know what Israel should do.’” The two versions attach different outcomes to the same tribes. Rav Tzadok specifically uses the second: victory over enemies and discriminating understanding.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 63:13 — “‘I will make you blood, and blood will pursue you; because you hated blood, blood will pursue you.’ Did Esav hate blood? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: This is the blood of the birthright and sacrifices. Rabbi Levi said: This is the blood of circumcision. The Sages said: You hated a person’s blood within his body.” The last explanation means that Esav did not let his victim’s blood remain within the body. It is the particular interpretation Rav Tzadok contrasts with Yosef’s sustaining other people.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 123b — “Rabbi Chelbo asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: ‘When Rachel had borne Yosef’—what changed when Yosef was born? He answered: Yaakov our father saw that Esav’s offspring are delivered only into the hands of Yosef’s offspring, as it says, ‘The house of Yaakov will be fire, the house of Yosef a flame, and the house of Esav straw.’” The Gemara explains Yaakov’s readiness to leave Lavan after Yosef’s birth. Rav Tzadok describes the moral reversal that makes Yosef the opposing force to Esav.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Chida, Chomas Anach, Emor — “‘Esav falls only by the hand of Rachel’s sons’: Yosef is the aspect of Yesod… and Yesod is shalom, which equals Esav in gematria, to nullify him.” The Chida gives a Kabbalistic reason for the Gemara Rav Tzadok cites. Yosef, the Yesod who “sustained” and made peace among the creatures, is the exact counterweight to Esav, the murderer and robber who “hated blood.”

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 19:3; Tanchuma, Chukas 6 — “‘Chalkol’—this is Yosef, as it says, ‘Yosef sustained’ his household. The Egyptians said: Did this slave reign over us through anything other than his wisdom? They brought seventy slips with seventy languages written on them, placed them before him, and he read each in its own language. Moreover, he spoke the holy language, which they could not understand.” The name Chalkol in I Melachim 5:11 is interpreted through Yosef’s provision of food. This passage is 19:3 in the retrieved Bamidbar Rabbah division; Tanchuma, Chukas 6, also preserves it.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 26a — “Rava said: You do not find a Torah scholar who renders authoritative instruction unless he comes from the tribe of Levi or Yissachar. Levi: ‘They will teach Your judgments to Yaakov.’ Yissachar: ‘Those who understand the times, to know what Israel should do.’ But why not Yehudah, since it says, ‘Yehudah is My lawgiver’? I am speaking of bringing a teaching to its conclusion according to the halachah.” The final answer identifies the special capacity at issue: reaching the correct halachic conclusion, rather than excluding the Torah learning of other tribes.

paragraphs.text: Tanchuma, Vayechi 11; Bereishis Rabbah 99:10 — “‘Yissachar is a strong-boned donkey’: Yissachar gives himself to Torah like a donkey to a burden, while Zevulun brings merchandise in ships. ‘Crouching between the boundaries’—these are his students, who spread Torah in Eretz Yisrael before the Sages. ‘He saw rest’—this is Torah. ‘That it was good’—this is Torah, as it says, ‘For I have given you good teaching.’ ‘He inclined his shoulder to bear’—the yoke of Torah.” Bereishis Rabbah gives the same burden-bearing comparison in the following paragraph after Zevulun, numbered 99:10 in the retrieved edition, rather than 99:9. The burden here is the chosen labor of Torah.

— “‘Yissachar is a strong-boned donkey’: Yissachar gives himself to Torah like a donkey to a burden, while Zevulun brings merchandise in ships. ‘Crouching between the boundaries’—these are his students, who spread Torah in Eretz Yisrael before the Sages. ‘He saw rest’—this is Torah. ‘That it was good’—this is Torah, as it says, ‘For I have given you good teaching.’ ‘He inclined his shoulder to bear’—the yoke of Torah.” Bereishis Rabbah gives the same burden-bearing comparison in the following paragraph after Zevulun, numbered 99:10 in the retrieved edition, rather than 99:9. The burden here is the chosen labor of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 5b — “Because the evil inclination distances a person from giving his money as tzedakah and from taking further trouble with the poor… one who does tzedakah this way has his inclination in his hand.” The Maharsha explains why chessed in particular subdues the yetzer. It demands both money and effort, the very things the inclination resists. This supports Rav Tzadok’s pairing of Yosef’s chessed with Yissachar’s Torah.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 5b — “‘Sending away the foot of the ox and the donkey’: The school of Eliyahu taught: A person should always set himself to the words of Torah like an ox to the yoke and a donkey to the burden.” The two animals now express chosen submission and labor. Rav Tzadok relates the yoke to the restraint of aggression and the burden to the discipline of desire.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Meir Leibush Weisser, Malbim on I Shmuel 15:2 — “His war had none of the reasons for which wars are ordinarily provoked. Its own cause was denial of God: after the peoples heard and trembled at the signs and wonders performed at the sea and in Egypt, he wished to fight Israel and demonstrate that Hashem could not save them. The main object of his war was thus opposition to Hashem. His hatred of Israel also arose from their ancestors, from Esav’s enmity toward Yaakov, since Amalek descended from Esav.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Malbim reaches this conclusion after excluding conquest, defense of borders, an existing quarrel, military reputation, and religious devotion as ordinary motives for the attack. That analysis clarifies Rav Tzadok’s precise claim that Amalek acted against reason despite the universal fear produced by the miracles; the issue is deliberate defiance of their divine source.

p: and this is the most brazen of all."
One may say that it alludes
to Amalek being the root of the evil inclination,
and can enter even a holy soul,
just as he dared to test and entice
and he is the beginning of the kelipah,
"Amalek is the first of the nations."
Keser Elyon is the Crown of Kingship
peace be upon him, is called "old" in holiness,
"And Avraham was old, advanced in days" —
בְּיוֹמִין עִלָּאִין [זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק א קכט, א]
in the supernal days (holy Zohar vol. 1, 129a) —
and he merited to be called "old"
כֵּן עֲמָלֵק נִקְרָא מֶלֶךְ זָקֵן וּכְסִיל
So Amalek is called "an old and foolish king
who no longer knows how to take heed,"
for he brazenly enters upon the greatest of the world,
"Beware of Rabbi Meir and his Torah;
beware of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah"
(as stated in Kiddushin 81a), as was said.
And this is what is said (I Shmuel 15:2):
"how he set upon him on the way
when he came up from Egypt" —
on which they went to receive the Torah;
and this is "when he came up from Egypt":
for besides having left the kelipos
leaving all ten crowns of impurity —
לְבַד זֶה הָיוּ עוֹלִין מַעְלָה מַעְלָה
besides this, they were ascending higher and higher;
and nevertheless he attached himself to them,
even though they surely proclaimed in heaven,
but he did not know how to take heed,
דָּרְשׁוּ וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹהִים עַל עֲמָלֵק
they expounded "and he did not fear G-d" as referring to Amalek.
וְלִכְאוֹרָה מַה זֶּה רְבוּתָא עַל עֲמָלֵק
Seemingly, what novelty is this regarding Amalek,
that he did not fear G-d?
But in Yisrael the fear of Hashem Yisbarach is
and among the nations of the world there is fear of punishment
and at the splitting of the Sea,
דִּכְתִיב [שְׁמוֹת טו, יד] שָׁמְעוּ עַמִּים יִרְגָּזוּן
where it is written (Shemos 15:14), "Nations heard and trembled,
there was at least fear of punishment.
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ אַף יִרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ
for he did not have even fear of punishment;
and this is his brazenness, as mentioned above.
Now the holiness of the three Avos
Avraham stands against the kelipah of Esav,
which is envy and hatred of people;
and Yitzchak Avinu, peace be upon him,
against the kelipah of Yishmael, lust
and the kelipah of Amalek is arrogance and honor,
"A man's pride will bring him low" (Mishlei 29:23) —
זֶה עֲמָלֵק שֶׁנִּתְגָּאָה עַל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵּי
this is Amalek, who exalted himself against HaKadosh Baruch Hu, etc.
בָּא לִידֵי חוּצְפָּה יְתֵירָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
he comes to excessive brazenness, as mentioned above.
וּלְעוּמָּתוֹ בִּקְדוּשָּׁה יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
Opposite him in holiness is Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
who said, "From where will my help come?"
וַעֲמָלֵק עָמַד בְּחוּצְפָּה נֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
Amalek stood brazenly against Hashem Yisbarach,
for he did not believe at all
that Hashem Yisbarach fights the war of Yisrael;
whereas Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, said,
"The G-d who has shepherded me all my life," etc.
for he did not perceive at all
that he accomplished anything by his own effort,
but said that everything is from Hashem Yisbarach.
וְנֶאֱמַר [עָמוֹס ז, ב] מִי יָקוּם יַעֲקֹב
And it says (Amos 7:2), "How will Yaakov stand,
which corresponds to Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
[פְּרִי עֵץ חַיִּים שַׁעַר הַשַּׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יז]
and "Shabbos: the shin is the secret of the three Avos,
and the bas is crowned with them"
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב רד, א)
for we merit the holiness of the Avos
when at the third meal we merit
the holiness of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
and the recognition that everything is from Hashem Yisbarach,
we say, "Outside they wander and do not enter,
for the kelipah of Amalek is nullified,
which is "the most brazen of all," as mentioned above.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Koheles 4:13 — “‘A poor and wise child’—this is the good inclination, called a child because it enters a person only at thirteen. ‘Poor’—because the limbs do not obey it as they obey the evil inclination. ‘Wise’—because it instructs a person in a good path. ‘Than an old and foolish king’—this is the evil inclination, which rules all the limbs. ‘Old’—because it is present from birth. ‘Foolish’—because it misleads him into a bad path. ‘Who no longer knows to take warning’—having grown old, he accepts no rebuke.” Rav Tzadok applies the verse’s three descriptions—king, old and foolish—to Amalek as the root of inner opposition.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 9 — “Just as in holiness Keser Elyon is crowned in Malchus… so in the kelipah the end is bound up in the beginning, and the primordial serpent is bound with the Nukva of the kelipah.” Rav Tzadok there takes up the same Zohar on the ox, the donkey and the dog (“kelev,” the reverse of “bakol”). He explains how Amalek can be both the “first” of kelipah and its lowest, insolent dog.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 26:3; Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 10 — “Why did Moshe send Yehoshua? He said to him: Your ancestor said, ‘I fear God,’ whereas of this one it says, ‘He did not fear God.’ Let the descendant of the one who said ‘I fear God’ come and exact payment from the one of whom it says ‘He did not fear God.’” Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 10, likewise contrasts Yosef’s fear with Esav’s lack of fear; Pesikta Rabbati 12 develops the inherited confrontation. The maamar’s reading of the phrase as Amalek’s fearlessness follows this strand of the Midrash.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 68:2 — “‘I lift my eyes to the mountains’—to the parents who taught and formed me. ‘From where will my help come?’ When Eliezer went to bring Rivkah, he took ten camels, whereas I have neither a ring nor a bracelet. Yaakov then said: Shall I lose my hope in my Creator? Heaven forbid! I will not lose my hope in my Creator. Rather, ‘My help is from Hashem.’” In the Midrash Yaakov’s lack of material resources becomes the occasion for reliance on Hashem. The maamar brings out its inner humility.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaShabbos 17, “From the companions” — “At Minchah he arranges four loaves and says: ‘This is the meal of Zeir Anpin, and the field of holy apples and Atika Kadisha come to dine with him.’ It corresponds to Yaakov, the father of seventy souls, and through his merit one is saved from the wars of Gog and Magog.” This is in the section headed “From the companions,” which assigns the evening meal to Yitzchak, the morning meal to Avraham, and the afternoon meal to Yaakov. The text later gives additional mystical configurations; the maamar cites this patriarchal correspondence.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Chaim of Volozhin, Nefesh HaChaim III:12 — “There is a great matter and wondrous means of removing and nullifying judgments and other wills, so that they cannot rule over a person or leave any impression. He establishes in his heart that Hashem is the true God, that no power exists anywhere in all the worlds apart from Him, and that everything is filled only with His simple unity. He inwardly nullifies all other powers, pays them no regard, and subjects and attaches the purity of his thought only to the one Master. He will then be enabled from above: the powers and wills of the world will fall away and be unable to act upon him.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Nefesh HaChaim describes the operative inward act in Rav Tzadok’s account of Yaakov: recognizing that all power belongs to Hashem entails relinquishing the imagined independence of other forces. It explains why Rav Tzadok treats humility and recognition that everything comes from Hashem as the means by which Amalek’s brazen opposing claim is excluded.
